author: Wajd
title: CPJ outraged by Egypt court conviction of journalist Lina Attalah, order of Mada Masr’s closure
content:
The Committee to Protect Journalists condemns the conviction of Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr, on charges of running an unlicensed website, and calls on Egyptian authorities to reverse the ruling, release the journalist immediately, and end their escalating campaign against independent journalism.

Mada Masr, among the first and few of Egypt’s independent media outlets, and a vital source of critical reporting, has long faced pressure from Egyptian authorities over its journalism. The outlet reported on Tuesday that the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court fined Attalah 3 million Egyptian pounds (about US$54,000), ordered the closure of the outlet, and the confiscation of its equipment. Attalah was subsequently taken into custody, and two Egyptian lawyers confirmed to CPJ that she will remain in custody until the fine is paid.

“The conviction of Lina Attalah and the order to shut down Mada Masr represent a devastating blow to press freedom in Egypt and a direct message aimed at dismantling independent media in the country,” said CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah. “Attalah and Mada Masr are among the most prominent voices in Egypt’s independent media landscape, providing critical reporting on issues of public interest that might otherwise go unreported. author: Amina Khan
title: EU transforms Frontex into a high-tech deportation command centre
content:
Yesterday, 27 October 2026, the European Commission tabled a new Regulation for Frontex, the EU’s border agency, expanding its powers and refocusing its mandate on deportations, preventing arrivals, and surveillance beyond EU territories and into social media. This would effectively turn Frontex into the EU’s deportation agency, equivalent of ICE in the United States.

At the centre of this reform is a budget that would almost double to nearly €12 billion for 2028–2034, leading to a massive expansion of the EU security and surveillance industrial complex. Frontex will test and deploy new technology to repress migrants, funnelling billions of taxpayer money to surveillance, security and defence contractors. EU’s hostile border security regime has for years produced systemic and massive human rights violations of migrants, refugees and racialised people, and those who stand in solidarity with them. This proposal will accelerate that.

Frontex as an ICE-style deportation enforcement agency

The proposal operationalises the recently adopted Deportations Regulation and deepens Frontex’s position as the central actor of a Europe-wide deportation machine. This will make the agency responsible for collecting and analysing data from Member States in order to “predict” deportation needs, and allocating resources to them. author: Access Now Advocacy Team
title: #NoExamShutdown: One step forward, another step back
content:
Every year, when exam season rolls around for students across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), many governments use the risk of cheating as an excuse to shut down the internet or block social media platforms. And every year, this results in millions of people losing connectivity, businesses grinding to a halt, and disruption to daily life across entire countries. Of course, exam shutdowns are not the only threat to education in the region; 

students in Gaza

 have begun a third academic year in tents and makeshift spaces, while in Lebanon, nearly 

100,000

 students were unable to return to school at all.




But across the wider MENA region, this year’s exam season saw mixed results for exam shutdowns. For the first time since Access Now, 

SMEX,

 and the 

Internet Society

 began tracking this phenomenon as part of the 

#NoExamShutdown campaign

, the trend went in two different directions across the map. For example, Algeria, which has been a persistent offender for the past decade, 

limited shutdown measures

 to the inside of exam centres, without disconnecting the rest of the country. Meanwhile Syria, which imposed 

11 nationwide exam-related shutdowns just last year

, appears to have held its 2026 exams without any documented disruptions. On the other hand, Tunisia — a country previously ranked as having the

author: Wajd
title: Urgent global call following the referral of Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah to trial
content:
Over a hundred civil society organizations and independent media outlets from around the world have come together to stand in solidarity with Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah following her referral to trial in Egypt.

We, the undersigned civil society organizations and independent media outlets from around the world, join together to condemn the unprecedented attack on press freedom in Egypt following the referral of Egyptian journalist and Editor-in-Chief of independent media outlet Mada Masr Lina Attalah to trial.

Just hours after Mada Masr joined seven other independent media outlets from across the Arab world in setting up a solidarity flash newsroom to fill the gap in coverage following the arrest of the entire newsroom of Egyptian investigative platform Matsadaash, on October 19, 2026, Lina Attalah received a summons to appear for questioning before the Supreme State Security Prosecution pending Case No. 9072 of 2026. The reasons for the summons were not disclosed.

At the interrogation, which took place on October 21 and lasted over six hours, Lina was questioned about Mada’s coverage on the wave of protests happening in prisons across the country, as well as the legal status of Mada Masr’s license. She was faced with charges of running a website without a license and of publishing false news with the aim of disturbing public peace and ultimately released on LE 10

author: Franco Giandana Gigena
title: Openness in AI development: a path to long-term independence
content:
As concerns grow over 

deepening dependencies

 on a handful of Big Tech companies and the 

outsized influence

 of the U.S. and China, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk used his speech during July’s inaugural 

Global Dialogue on AI Governance

 to call on humans to 

“take back our agency”

 over AI. But what does agency over AI really mean? What policies and practices can allow people to shape AI in ways that respect, rather than undermine, 

human rights

? 




This blog post unpacks concrete initiatives that show how openness in AI development can increase people’s agency over AI and advance the development of public interest technology. At the same time, we reflect on how openness is not the same thing as mere access, and how short-term pragmatism can pave the way toward long-term independence.




Why is AI development so concentrated? 




Last year, the UN formally established an 

Independent International Scientific Panel on AI

, intended to “advance scientific understanding and ensure that international deliberations are informed by the best available evidence.” The panel’s 

preliminary report

title: Deliberately forgotten: internet shutdowns with no end
content:
Content note: The following post contains references to war crimes, sexual assault, murder, and death

.







There is a complete lack of transparency.










Cutting the internet means cutting us off from the outside world.










I can say that the internet and communications blackout were as impactful as the bombings, destruction, and killings.










These are the words of people who have experienced years-long 

internet shutdowns with no end in sight

. Alarmingly, the number of such prolonged shutdowns has steadily risen each year, as perpetrators around the world quietly decide to 

keep people cut off from the internet indefinitely

.

control and surveillance of communications networks

internet dead zone

” where few dare to speak openly against the regime. In Tigray, Ethiopia, meanwhile, 

new internet shutdowns

 are raising fears that the same population that was 

cut off from the internet for over two years during a bloody civil war
